The Kremlin is dismissing independent media investigations that claim Russia's battlefield
losses in Ukraine run as high as 700,000 soldiers.
As NPR's Charles Mains reports, the findings are based on data allegedly stolen from Russian
government servers.
The data was obtained by Ukrainian and Belarusian hacker groups that claimed to have infiltrated
Russia's state statistics agency, and then distributed what they stole to a handful of
Russian independent news outlets operating in exile.
Their subsequent research found Russia registered nearly half a million military deaths by September
2026.
However, several outlets projected the real number was much higher, over 700,000, once
delays in entering data and soldiers missing but presumed dead were factored in.
The Kremlin spokesman urged the public to ignore the findings, saying only Russia's
defense ministry could be trusted with information on war losses.
Yet that ministry last announced casualty figures in September of 2022, when it said
nearly 6,000 troops had been killed in battle.
Charles Mains, NPR News, Moscow.
In Israel, judges are calling to drop some of the corruption charges against Prime Minister
Benjamin Netanyahu.
The trial against him has been going on for six years, and he denies wrongdoing.
Here's Daniel Estrin, has more from Tel Aviv.
In a surprise move, the judges overseeing Netanyahu's corruption trial called on Israel's
attorney general to consider dropping the most serious case of bribery, where Netanyahu
was accused of trading business favors with a media mogul in exchange for positive news
coverage.
In the second case involving Netanyahu's dealings with a newspaper owner, the judges
said they doubted a crime was committed, and the judges recommended the sides settle the
final case, where Netanyahu is accused of getting gifts from a Hollywood producer and
helping him with an Israeli tax break.
This is promising news for Netanyahu, but he may be unseated as Prime Minister as early
as next week.
His rival, Gadi Eisenkot, is trying to form a new government.
Daniel Estrin, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
